power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: TNF Tumor necrosis factor GM-CSF Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor MSMD DHR Dihydrorhodamine TEMRA T effector memory re-expressing CD45RA MAIT Mucosal-associated invariant T NK Natural killer DC Dendritic cell
Two otherwise healthy patients from Colombia, now aged 30 and 38 years, developed pulmonary tuberculosis due to inherited, complete TNF deficiency at the ages of 19 and 18 years.
We report here a previously healthy Iranian patient with inherited complete TNF deficiency who was diagnosed with both pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB between 10 and 15 years of age.
The homozygous TNF variant (c.673C>T) introduces a premature stop codon (TNF p.Q225*) resulting in losses of expression and function.
text.formatted: The homozygous TNF variant (c.673C>T) introduces a premature stop codon (TNF p.Q225*) resulting in losses of expression and function.

text.text: Despite normal myeloid and lymphoid subset development, the patient's primary leukocytes do not secrete detectable amounts of TNF.
As in the TNFdeficient Colombian patients, the respiratory burst of GM-CSF-derived macrophages is impaired.

Our findings expand the spectrum of TB phenotypes in patients with TNF deficiency and confirm that TNF is essential for immunity to M. tuberculosis in humans but apparently redundant against many other pathogens, including weakly virulent mycobacteria.
Tuberculosis (TB) is most frequently triggered by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tb) 1 .
text.formatted: Tuberculosis (TB) is most frequently triggered by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tb) <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">1</ref> .

text.text: A quarter of the world's population is latently infected with M. tb 1 .
text.formatted: A quarter of the world's population is latently infected with M. tb <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">1</ref> .

text.text: In 5-10% of cases, infection progresses to active TB, which remains the leading infectious cause of death worldwide 1 .

text.text: Discoveries of the genetic etiologies underlying Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (MSMD), characterized by susceptibility to weakly virulent mycobacteria and the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine (an attenuated live strain of Mycobacterium bovis) 2 , were instrumental in demonstrating that TB can also be a monogenic disorder in some patients 3, 4 .

text.text: Indeed, genetic defects disrupting interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) immunity have been reported in patients with TB.

Biallelic genotypes involving rare variants of TNF 5 , LY9 6 , ITK 7 , IL12RB1 8 , IL23R 9 , SPPL2A 10 and 11 and the common variants IL23R R381Q 9 and TYK2 P1104A 12 have all been reported to underlie TB.

text.text: Human genetics studies have clearly shown that the protection against TB provided by host immunity is dependent on an intact IFN-γ circuit, including the molecules inducing IFN- and those induced by IFN-, to eliminate the mycobacteria within macrophages.

Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) is a pro-inflammatory cytokine produced by macrophages in response to IFN-γ; it drives inflammation, promotes cell death and activates the respiratory burst mediated by the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) during infection 5, 13 .

text.text: IFN-γ can therefore drive ROS production both directly and indirectly, by upregulating the transcription of the NADPH oxidase components involved in the respiratory burst 14 and inducing the production of TNF 15.

text.text: In this context, we previously described two patients with TB from the same Colombian family with inherited, complete TNF deficiency 5 .

text.text: TNF has been implicated in host defense against multiple pathogens in mice 16 , but these two patients presented with recurrent pulmonary TB, despite broad pathogen exposure, including BCG vaccination.

text.text: They were homozygous for a private TNF variant underlying complete TNF loss-of-function (LOF) 5 .

text.text: They developed TB at the ages of 19 and 18 years.
They are now 30 and 38 years of age, respectively, in complete remission, and healthy.
TNF deficiency weakened antimycobacterial defense at the cellular level, by impairing the respiratory burst in GM-CSF-matured and alveolar macrophages 5 , but not in neutrophils.

text.text: This observation is consistent with rare CYBB variants selectively impairing ROS production in macrophages and leading to MSMD, a phenotype largely restricted to mycobacterial disease [17] [18] [19] .

text.text: By contrast, patients with chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) have a broad clinical phenotype due to the impairment of ROS production in all phagocytes 20 .

text.text: We searched for new patients with autosomal recessive (AR) TNF deficiency, to expand our allelic, clinical and cellular understanding of TNF deficiency.
We studied a female patient (P) born to consanguineous parents from Iran (Figure 1A).
text.formatted: We studied a female patient (P) born to consanguineous parents from Iran (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1A</ref>).

text.text: She was diagnosed with miliary pulmonary TB (between 10-15 years of age) with dissemination to the left pelvic bone, presenting with fever, fatigue, muscle pain, and an unexplained loss of about 3 kg of body weight.
Acid-fast microscopy on a sputum sample revealed the presence of M. tb., and a tuberculin purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test with 5 tuberculin units resulted in an induration of 25 mm.
These tests were also performed on the patient's parents and sibling, yielding negative results.
CT scans of the patient's lungs were indicative of miliary TB (Figure 1B).
text.formatted: CT scans of the patient's lungs were indicative of miliary TB (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1B</ref>).

text.text: At the time of diagnosis, immunological profiling showed the patient to have essentially normal proportions of leukocytes.
The patient had a leukocyte count of 8800/mm 3 , with the proportions of neutrophils (36%), eosinophils (5.3%), and lymphocytes (45%) all within the normal range.
The 102 proportion of monocytes was slightly high, at 12%.
Acute-phase reactant levels were high, with a 103 C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 63 mg/liter.

The patient received a three-month course 104 of anti-TB treatment with a five-drug regimen consisting of isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, 105 levofloxacin, and clarithromycin, followed by nine additional months of treatment with isoniazid 106 and rifampin, leading to complete recovery.
The patient was vaccinated with BCG at birth, without 107 adverse effects, and none of her relatives had any history of TB.
The patient was also diagnosed 108 with hypothyroidism and is currently being treated with levothyroxine.
She was otherwise healthy 109 and is HIV-negative.
No autoantibodies against IFN-, IL-12, IL-23 or TNF were detected in the 110 patient's serum.
No other unusual infections were reported.

Serological testing (Table 1) and 111 VirScan analysis (Figure 1C) of the patient confirmed normal antibody repertoires against 112 common pathogens, such as human coronavirus OC43, cytomegalovirus, and norovirus, 113 demonstrating intact T cell and B cell functions for seroconversion after vaccination and immunity 114 to common infections.

text.text: Overall, these data suggest that complete TNF deficiency did not alter the development of the major myeloid and lymphoid subsets in the blood.
We report a new patient with inherited TNF deficiency as a genetic etiology of TB, confirming the importance of TNF as a non-redundant component of human immunity to M. tb.

The defects observed in this patient are consistent with our findings for other TNF-deficient patients 5 , in whom impaired TNF signaling leads to defective ROS production in GM-CSF-matured MDMs ex vivo, with broader myeloid and lymphoid differentiation remaining intact.

text.text: This dissociation between the preservation of hematopoietic development and selective effector dysfunction highlights a specialized role for TNF in macrophage antimicrobial programming rather than in immune lineage specification.

Collectively, these data support a mechanistic model in which TNF is crucial for the optimization of macrophage bactericidal activity via ROS-dependent pathways to provide essential protection against M. tb infection.

Our findings for this patient extend the genetic and clinical field of TNF deficiency-associated TB to new geographic and ethnic backgrounds, adding an Iranian individual to the previously reported Colombian cases, thereby increasing the generalizability of TNF deficiency as a monogenic cause of TB.

A highly consistent immunological phenotype was observed in all the reported patients: preserved resistance to the agent used for BCG vaccination and to a range of other common intracellular pathogens, including environmental and atypical mycobacteria, but with selective susceptibility to M. tb.

This pattern suggests that TNF is not broadly required for host defense against most pathogens, instead playing a more specific role in optimizing antimycobacterial effector mechanisms, particularly those linked to ROS generation in GM-CSF-matured macrophages.
Unlike the previously reported Colombian patients, who had primarily pulmonary disease, this patient had disseminated TB, with lesions in her left pelvic bone.
TB is the most lethal human infectious disease worldwide 1 , reflecting the ability of M. tb to exploit vulnerabilities in host immunity.
It is, therefore, unsurprising that any impairment of ROS production by TNF deficiency, which is crucial for macrophage function, renders the host susceptible to severe TB.
Conversely, it is surprising that TNF deficiency results in a selective susceptibility to TB disease and not to other pathogens, including weakly virulent mycobacteria.
